utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. This is Tuesday, April 22nd, 2008, and I welcome Mr. Marcussen, our witness, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the other people helping us. I would like to ask Madam Registrar to please move to private session in order for the solemn declaration to be made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have with me first -- I should introduce my assistant today, one of our interns, Amy Sinier, who is helping with the presentation of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, what religion do you have, if you have any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I grew up in the village of Divic, Zvornik Municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you live there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority population were Muslim in the village. There were some Serbs, one family and five people from a mixed marriage, married to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many people lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly, two and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the Muslims and the few people of Serb origin that lived in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the relations were good. I don't think there were any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to talk about first some events in the beginning of April 1992. Around that time, did you see any military equipment in the area that were not usually there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps at the beginning of 1992, it was noticed on the Serb side that there was some artillery pieces, artillery weapons, that weren't there beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you say "on the Serb side," what do you mean? The Serb side of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Serbian side of -- of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Divic is at the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, in the border area, so what I mean is on the side of the state of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what -- is the border visible by any particular natural feature? Maybe I can help the witness out -- maybe I can lead on this. I think it's a matter of just confusing -- am I correct that the border is demarcated by the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the artillery pieces you see -- you saw, at some point were they stationed at particular locations that were recognisable along the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were positioned at the bridges and opposite to where I lived, on a hill there. I think it was in Mali Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, if you can try to speak a little bit louder. It's difficult for the interpreters to hear you. After Zvornik was attacked on around the 8th of April, did the inhabitants of your village remain in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not at that time, not everybody remained. Perhaps a couple of people stayed on. The rest left and went to the neighbouring villages, around the village of Divic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You, yourself, did you stay or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also left one night, and then I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what about your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family stayed for several days, stayed up there, and then a couple of days later my father returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you have other members of your family living in your village with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some time, everybody went back to the village of Divic, those who wanted to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after people had returned, what was the situation like in Divic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, the situation was -- well, we were isolated. We couldn't go into town anymore. We were there in the place we were in, and we weren't allowed to move around, we couldn't move around, just around those villages and perhaps take the road to a little further off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to jump a little bit ahead to the month of May, and I'd like to ask you: Did there come a time when the inhabitants of your village were asked to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That happened roughly around the 26th of May, after the units -- the shifts of the units were changed who were in our place on the Serb side, this unit came in and the unit said we had to move out because nobody could guarantee our safety and security there any longer. And they gave us roughly two hours to get ready, to prepare ourselves, and then they said they would transport us to Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The unit that moved into your village, could you describe that unit for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the army, soldiers wearing military uniforms. We didn't know the unit -- we didn't know the people, rather. I didn't know them, didn't know who they were. So, well, they all had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why do you identify them as being from the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were wearing military uniforms, and at the beginning, when the Serb army came to our village, after that first military unit that entered our village, the police came. I think it was the police from the town of Zvornik, and it patrolled the area, and in a way it allowed us or enabled us to go into town. And in town, we would be issued permits allowing us to move around. So they were in blue uniforms, and that's why I think that unit was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And so you said that you were told that you would be transported to Olovo. How many people were going to be transported, do you estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 500 people, a total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How were you going to be transported, by what means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were 11 buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you go to Olovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never reached Olovo. We reached Han Pijesak, and we weren't able to go further on from there, because they told us that there was fighting going on up ahead so we weren't allowed to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the place where you couldn't move on from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there for approximately two hours, and then we returned, and we were stopped between Vlasenica and Milici. I think the place was actually called Zaklopaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how long were you stopped at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the next day, did you move on again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, we once again set out in the direction of Zvornik, where we were stopped by the SUP of Zvornik, and we spent about an hour there. And then we set off again in the direction of Tuzla, and we reached Crni Vrh, and we weren't able to go further because allegedly there was some fighting going on there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so having been stopped again, where did you -- where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sent us back to the Zvornik station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What kind of a station; train station, bus station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what happened there at the bus station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waited there for a time, and then some soldiers turned up, some young guys wearing uniforms, and they ordered all the men to step out of the buses, and they escorted us to the city stadium that was right next to the station. And up on the stands, they separated people, people over the age of 65 and those under the age of 18, and then they returned them to the buses. And then these men, who were militarily fit, stayed on the stands. The others were returned to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many people remained on the stands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 174 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were among those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where were this group of men that you were in -- where were you taken from the bus station -- from the stadium, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us in column, two-by-two, away from the stadium. They escorted us through town to the administration building at Novi Izvor [Realtime transcript read in error "Mali Izvor"], where they put us up in a room there, and we had enough space just to stand, standing room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And while you were there, were you -- did anybody of authority come to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some time had gone by, Brano Grujic turned up. I think he was an official in the Zvornik Municipality, and he said we would go and do some labour somewhere and that we should draw up a list of the people in the room and sign it -- or, rather, sign a loyalty oath or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Loyalty to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, to their authorities. What he had in mind, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say "their authorities," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb authorities. Or, rather, I think that it meant that we should accept their power and authority. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you sign the loyalty certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, and I don't think anybody else did, because they no longer asked for it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I move on, at page 9, line 20 of the transcript, there's a reference to a location which should be Novi Izvor. N-O-V-I I-Z-V-O-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Witness 1065, at this point in time did any of the men that you were with leave the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After some time had gone by, they took out a young man, and later on we learnt that through the intervention of his family from Serbia, they transported him to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And later on, did more -- did more people leave the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After time, some young guys turned up, wearing military uniforms, and they said that they were looking for 10 volunteers who would go with them to our village to search the houses there, and then allegedly they would return and another group would be sent out until all the houses had been searched and until they all went back to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did any of those men come back again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, 11 people went, and they never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, have they been seen since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think anybody saw them alive, but they were found dead, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name -- the names of any of these 10 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was Enver Pezerovic, Smajl Pezerovic, Kemal Tuhcic, Hasan Tuhcic, Ibrahim Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, you -- did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yesterday, did you have a chance to review that statement again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in that statement, did you list the names of the victims that you remembered had suffered various abuses and were killed during the time period that we are talking about today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you looked at your statement yesterday, did that -- did that remind you of the victims that you knew about had suffered abuses and who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were you shown a list of various victims yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And having looked at that list, did you make some corrections to the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the list that you were shown was a list of various victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in addition to making corrections to the lists, did you also add some additional victims that were not included in your statement from 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And having done that, was the list then corrected and updated based on the corrections you had made to the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask now if we could call up 65 ter number 7220.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Witness 1065, now on your screen, to your right, there should be a picture of a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to -- the English version, if we could look at the bottom part of the document. Sorry, can we move away from that again, please. I should probably ask that we do not broadcast the exhibit outside the courtroom, if we can avoid that. So that's not been done. Sorry, can we move back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, is this the list that was finalised with you yesterday, and is this your signature down at the bottom there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could we move to the next page, please, of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is difficult to see, but is this also your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The same exercise again to the third page. Go down and see the signature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, again, this is also your signature on the third page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And let's do the last two pages as well. If we can go to the fourth page. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the last page, if we can go to that and have a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, again, am I correct this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like at this stage to seek the admission of this list of victims. I'm going to come back to the list a number of times as we move through the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just one question. You put your signature at the bottom of various lists of victims. We have this list. Therefore, I am slightly taken aback by the fact that you can give names of more than 100 people. You give their first names, their last names. Should we think that when you came to The Hague, you already had on you, in your pocket, let's say, a list of victims' names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list of all those persons that are contained in my statement was given during my first statement in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to 1996, because I have your statement in my hand, there were 11 people who disappeared. They must have been killed. And now we have 26 names. So you've added 15 names. Did your memory just come back, or how can you explain this additional knowledge? Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. If you will allow me to explain the logic of the list, that is the Prosecutor's making and not the witness. The list has been drawn up, so there are basically four parts of the list that talk about different series of events, one series of events prior to the Bajram holiday, events on the Bajram holiday, events on the Vidovdan holiday, and events at the Batkovic camp. So we're trying, in the list, to group the victims together. So the 11 people that are mentioned by the victims are on the list, but there are other victims that were killed during the pre-Bajram period following these 11 people. But I will be going through that with the witness in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor explained to us how this list came about. This list, the Prosecutor tells us that he drafted it and subdivided the list in three categories; the victims before Bajram, the victims during Bajram, and we have the victims after Bajram. This is why the lists that you signed show us all the victims' names. Do you agree with what the Prosecutor just explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Marcussen. Would you like to have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number P381.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have asked that it be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P381, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065 -- oh, sorry, could we go back to the first page of this exhibit. If we look at this list, the 11 people that you mentioned were taken away from the Novi Izvor administrative building, are they, on this -- can you see them on this page, and if so, which numbers do they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are on this list from numbers 1 to 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there for about three days in the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we were told to leave the building, and they transferred us by buses to a nearby place on the road between Zvornik and Bijeljina. The place was called Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like now if we could call up Exhibit 65 ter 4164, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the building where we were put up after the administrative building and Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So is this the building in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this was -- picture was not included in -- by mistake was not included in the witness binder. I would like to show another picture for the witness and ask him what the picture is, and that is 65 ter number 4148, which is a picture that was in the witness binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, do you know what this building is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same building in Celopek, in front of the centre. It was the bus station at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 65 ter number 4164 and 4148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 4164 becomes P382 and 4148 becomes P383.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the Registrar, we will be talking more about the list, so P81, under seal, during the rest of the testimony, so maybe you want to prepare that as we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, how big was the room that you were placed in in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was like a cinema hall. I can't tell you exactly, but about 20 metres wide and some 50 metres long, perhaps a little smaller or a little bigger than that. I must say that I'm not quite certain when talking about widths and lengths, and I don't know the exact size of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there anything prepared there for the detainees to be able to sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived or, rather, entered this hall, we saw that there were about eight iron beds there and thin field mattresses, some blankets, and there was a stage on the right-hand side of the building, so that almost all of us had somewhere to lie down and to cover ourselves with the blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you given any food while you were detained there in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first three days, we didn't get anything as food. We had to manage somehow ourselves, with the help of the guards who were there. We'd give them some money and they would get us something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the guards that were there, could you describe how they looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing blue uniforms. They were armed. They had automatic rifles. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move outside the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we could go out in front of the building. We could go and use the toilet without any problems. We could come out when we liked, to light a cigarette, except during the night. But later on, we couldn't go out without permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did the guards change at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards who were in front of the building were always members of the police. I think it was the municipal police. I don't know exactly who they were. But occasionally some others would come, some other groups or some other men, who were wearing military uniforms or half civilian, half military clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when -- no, sorry, let me rephrase that. At the beginning, did you have your ID papers and other personal belongings with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only had the clothes we were wearing on us. As for the document, a savings booklet and everything, we had that on us, but we had no luggage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you -- your personal papers taken away from you at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think early on, a day or two later, a group of men arrived, who ordered us to take off our belts, shoelaces, and they took away all our documents and everything we had. We had to hand in money, jewellery, documents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And these men, could you describe what they looked like? Were they members of the police or were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniform. The colour was green, SMB, the military colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said that you had to hand in all your personal papers, and your shoelaces and belts and money. Was anyone asked to pay money to this group later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They took out a person, and they promised him that they would transfer him to where he wanted to go, and he was told to give him about 2.000 German marks, and for this sum they would transfer him to wherever he said he wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he have 2.000 marks that he could give the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't have that money on him. He asked us to lend him the money, and he said he would return the money when he was freed. However, the people who had money collected about 1.700 marks for him to be able to give the money to this group that was demanding it of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did he give the money to the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he handed over the money. And later on, when they came, at the time they promised the money was given to them, he asked that they return at least our IDs. And during the first conversation, they promised to do that. Later on, when he handed over the money and when he asked for those documents, they swore at him, they hit him and pushed him back into the room where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who were asked to give the 2.000 marks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name was Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask that we go into private session just for a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, did there come a time when a registration was made of some of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were staying in this room, at the beginning, almost every evening, the people were counted who were there, and a list of names was made, I think, only once, but the numbers were checked every evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the making of the list, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to form two lines, and then a policeman came, wearing a blue uniform, who counted the men, who checked whether everyone was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there a point when the detainees were asked to make a list, themselves, or write down names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, we were asked to make a list of fathers and sons who were there in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who asked you to make that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, a group came who introduced themselves as being the people who would take care of us, who would, as they said, protect us, that the only requirement was that we carry out their orders. They didn't give their names. They just told us a song that we had to sing when they came and when they left. And from this song, we concluded that the name of one of them was Repic, or rather his nickname. And also from that song, we assumed that the other person's nickname was Lopov or "thief."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did Repic have anything to do with the order that you prepare a list of fathers and sons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told us, for fathers and sons, to separate, and first the sons had to form a line and then their father stood behind them, and then we had to make that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were any of the detainees that were registered marked in some way at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were making the list, he went from one person to the other and he made a cross on the forehead of some men with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was a cross made on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That didn't happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many men had a cross made on their forehead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think roughly about 10. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'm afraid I misled the Registrar a little while ago. I think we have to go and see 65 ter number 4216.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is Repic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I saw the photograph in the file. Could you tell us where it comes from? Where did you get this photograph? What is its source?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's a photograph that -- it's a still or two stills that are taken from a video, and I haven't had time to check what that video is. I have the video reference to it. But it's a video -- a still that the Office of the Prosecutor has taken from a video, and it was -- it was referred to in the statement of the witness from 1996, at page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But this video, is it the recording of a questioning by the police? I guess so. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I haven't had time to check on the video. I can inform you, after the break, what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number P384.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you have described one group, and you have given the nicknames of some of the members of this group. Was there another group that also came to where you were detained regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did come. Those others who came weren't called by their names. There was one they referred to as "Major," and the other one's name was Zoks. Now, I learnt of this name later on, when we went to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The person you learned was called "Zoks," have you subsequently seen him? And I ask that you just answer "yes" or "no" to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd ask we move into private session for the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On the day that Zoks and his group came to where you were detained, did anything particular happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time they arrived, those groups arrived, something happened. And when Zoks arrived and this major -- well, they referred to him as "Major," they asked us to hand over our money, our weapons. And on many occasions, they asked us to hand over our weapons or to tell them who was in possession of weapons, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did anyone say anything about how much value were put on your lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while they were asking for these weapons or money, they would threaten us and say that they'd kill us. They threatened us in various ways, and then they -- or, rather, Zoks said to us that our lives were cheaper than the bullet in the barrel in the pistol he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were [sic] anyone actually killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anybody actually killed, but two people were taken out, and you could hear two shots fired. And afterwards, they took out another person to see what had happened outside -- I apologise for coughing -- to see what had happened outside. And when that person returned to the room, they told him to tell us what he had seen. Now, he couldn't do that or wouldn't do that to begin with, but as they forced him then he said that the people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The person who was taken outside and came back and told this to the other detainees, do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Sakib.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the names of the two people that were killed, do you remember those today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramo and Sulejman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd ask if we could call up the list that we saw before. So I believe that was P381. The list is up to the left on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The two people you just mentioned, are they on this list? And if so, what number do they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he's [as interpreted] under number 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were anyone else called out that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they took out I think his name was Alija. They took him outside and brought him back, but he didn't tell us what they asked of him. And then they selected a young man whom they took out, and they talked to him. I don't know what they talked to him about. And that young man afterwards, when they returned him, he said in front of them -- he told us -- he said that we should say -- we should say who of us had weapons to save his life, because they told him that he would be killed unless we told him who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- well, could you describe, then, what happened during -- in a general way, what happened during the following days? Did these groups come back to you in -- where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those groups were there almost all the time on the premises. Now, perhaps there were times in between where we were left to ourselves, but otherwise those groups would be there. They would rotate, they would change shifts. Sometimes they were together, other times they were separate, but they were there almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they -- were they there as guards or did they do something else to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they were there in the capacity of guards. I think they would come in from somewhere else, and they would come because of their interests; either to make fun of us, or take our money, or things like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about Dihic, Enes and Halilovic, Ibro. Do you know these two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do know those two. They were taken out by Repic on one occasion while Repic was looking for money, asking us to hand over any money we might have. And while they were beating us and God knows what else they were doing to us, he took Enes out first and he said that he had to talk to him about something. And then the people who were with him, they threw Enes out. Then afterwards he selected Ibro. He took him out, too. And they never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you about a person that -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, there's something here that I find strange in your answers. There's a group of persons coming to -- asking you for money. Actually, it's racketing, in a way. Why can't they just search everyone and take the money that people would have on them, rather than ask for money and then hit people? Do you have an opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said a moment ago that the first group which came and which ordered us to hand over all the documents, and our belts, and anything else, we did that, we handed all those things over, and they didn't hand over everything because the people -- some people thought that it wouldn't last long and that they might need some money. But when they took out the second person and asked for money in order to transfer him to another place, well, he collected this sum of money, so I think that they realised that people still had some money on them. That's what they thought, so they demanded that it be handed over. So that might have been the reason, or perhaps the reason was that they wanted to do what they intended to do in the first place, and that was a sort of pretext.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Marcussen, please resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, I'm unsure about the exact time we are here. Could you just clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, I know it's difficult to keep track of precise dates, but could you tell us approximately when the events you're talking about now took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those events took place, let's say, perhaps a week after -- one or two weeks after our arrival, after we were put in that room. So that was the period, let's say, before Bajram. Afterwards, it was the 10th and 11th, and it was the Bajram holiday, and that's when some more serious incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, Cupcic [phoen], Ismet, is that a person that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Ismail Topcic. Repic went up to the man and took him by his ear. He wanted to cut it off with a knife. He put a knife to it and told him to hand over his money and tell who else had money, and he started to cry. He said he didn't know, he said he didn't have any money, so that he would leave him alone. But Repic just cut the ear a little bit and left him alone. He didn't touch him anymore after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about a person with a nickname of Buco. Do you know a person referred to by that nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Buco, the person with that nickname, I learned of that name in Batkovici. That's when I heard it. It was a largely-built man, strongly-built man, or perhaps rather fat, and the person would come with Zoks' group. He turned up with Zoks' group. And that person also stuck knives or a knife into people's thighs, and he cut off a person's finger, poked the knife into the person's hand and arm, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he do that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He also stabbed me in both hands and cut into my shoulder, left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you have scars from that today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask if we could go into private session for again a brief minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I believe that you have about 50 to 55 minutes left. I'm just telling you for your information, so you can prepare for the next questions after the break. But it is now 10.30, and we will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back into open session. But before we resume, the Chamber will read a short oral decision regarding the lifting of the confidentiality for the transcript. I will read slowly. Given the oral motion presented by the accused on the 10th of April, 2008, regarding the publication of portions of the transcript which took place in private session on that same day, given that the Chamber considers that the confidentiality of some portions of the transcript identified hereunder can be lifted while respecting the confidentiality of the witness, and I will read the relevant portions which are now public. Page 5968, line 13, to page 5972, line 7. And then pages 5982, line 28, to page 5988, line 2. Then page 5988 [Realtime transcript read in error "5998"], line 12, to page 59 -- there's a mistake in the transcript. From pages 5988, line 12, to page 5989, line 4. The references to the transcript are also the references in the French transcript. Very well. This being said, Mr. Marcussen, we've talked earlier about the Belgrade trial. The Trial Chamber would like to have in its possession a copy of the indictment or what replaces an indictment in the local jurisdiction regarding the six accused of the trial that is now taking place. We would like to have it as soon as possible, please. Another thing that we would like to ask the Prosecution, and I would like to ask of this in private session -- could we please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I promised to try to find out where the still photographs that were shown earlier to the witness come from, and I understand that it is a still that is taken from a video that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Witness VS-27, who had been preparing a documentary, and it's from that material that this particular still has been taken. We, of course, hope to have VS-27 here and to be able to clarify the origin of this with him, but that's the information I have at this stage about the source of that particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1067 -- 1065, we're now back in open session. After the events that we talked about while we were in private session, what happened to the detainees in the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were there, as these groups changed, as I described a moment ago, people were mistreated in the way I have described. Then some of those people were taken out, and they never came back. Some people were taken out to see what had happened outside, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if you would look at the list that you have in front of you on the screen. The people that you just mentioned that were taken out and never came back, are they found on this page of the list? And if so, with what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are on the list. We said a moment ago that numbers 12, 13, 14, 15 were taken out and they didn't come back. The person under number 16 also was taken out and didn't come back. The persons under 17, 18, 19 were also taken out, taken away, and they didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the three people that are mentioned under 17, 18 and 19, do you know whether they were related in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those three persons were three brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you know who took them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken out by Repic's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And sorry, I interrupted you. If you wouldn't mind continuing down the list, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person under number 20 was also taken out and he didn't come back. The persons under 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26 were also taken out, and they didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on, then, to Bajram day. Could you tell us what happened on that day? And if you can start just describing the day, and then we'll probably have to go into private session in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I don't remember the time when this happened, a group came -- or, rather, this Repic man entered, and he asked us, as he had done before, to talk about certain persons that he named. And he asked whether we would write to him or tell him something about that. Then he asked that fathers and sons come out. Some of those persons came out. He sent them to the stage. After that, I think he noticed that they were too few. Then he started selecting people, himself, the men he wanted to choose, and they were sent to the stage too. And then he ordered those men to get ready, and the others who were in the room were ordered to move to one side and to sit down. And the people who were on the stage had to take off their clothes and were forced to engage in oral sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many people were on the stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many. I think there were two pairs of father and son and perhaps about ten people in all. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would request if -- that we move to the third page of the exhibits on the screen, provided that we still are in a setting where the exhibit is not being shown outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, without stating any names, on the page that you now see before you, do you see the names of some of the people that were on the stage who were forced to perform these acts? And if so, with what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those men are under numbers 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. After this event, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were ordered to engage in oral sex, Repic walked around in front of us and selected people who he would shoot at. At first, I thought it was an air rifle, but when I saw that people were dying, that people hit in the eye lost their eye, so I realised that it was a different kind of weapon, a small-calibre rifle. I don't know much about these things, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, do you -- do you know the name of any of the people who got killed? And if so, do you see them on the list in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are on the list of men who were killed in the room. They are under numbers 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. A brief moment in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What happened to the bodies of the people that had been killed by Repic, as you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After completing this act, if I can put it that way, we had to carry out -- the men outside. I didn't go out; I stayed inside. Those bodies were loaded onto a truck and were taken in an unknown direction. We had to clean up everything so there wouldn't be any traces of blood, so that no one could notice that something had happened. So all this was done by two groups. In the first group were the men killed, and in the second group there was a couple of bodies and the bed clothes and blankets that were bloodied, and we had to clean it all up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- the men who were carrying out the bodies, did they come back into the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those men never came back, never came back to this room where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The name of those people who went out and did not come back, are they found on the list? And if so, under what numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are under numbers 48, 49, 50, 51, and 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you tell us what happened to the person listed under number 53?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person under number 53 was taken out after all these others had been taken away, and the people who accompanied the dead men. He was taken out, and one of us saw him cleaning up something outside. He also didn't come back into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Again, I'd ask for a brief moment in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you -- did you know a person named Pezerovic, Zaim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also lived in our village, and he was detained with us in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you tell us if anything happened to him around the time we are just talking about now, well, on Bajram day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day when all these things were happening, I'm referring to the oral sex and the murder of these men, a while later Repic took out two men. Zaim was one of them and Sakib was the other. He chose those two and told them to lie down. I couldn't see properly what happened to them, but I heard from others that one had his throat slit and the other was stabbed in the heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Sakib, do you know what his family name is or was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kapidzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you witness anyone else being stabbed by Repic that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the two of them, he climbed on to the stage and he ordered Saban Bikic to lie down on the stage, and he also stabbed him in the chest, in the heart. He left his knife there, and this person tried to pull the knife out, probably to save himself, but he didn't succeed and he was -- stayed there dead on the stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There are two -- number 57 and number 58 on the list that you have in front of you. Do you know what happened to those two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those two persons were killed on the stage with this small-calibre rifle or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Repic did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Apart from the people whose names we have been talking about today, were there other people that were killed that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that on that same day, I don't think there were others killed except the ones I mentioned, but there were visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say "there were visits," what happened during those visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I say "visits," I mean these groups coming in to where we were, who replaced each other but who were there almost all the time, and the events that we've been talking about; that they beat us, that they cut us with knives, that they killed us, that they forced us to perform oral sex, and all the other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, beaten by Repic or by his group on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whether it was actually on that particular day or a minute before or a day before, I can't say, but, anyway, we all had to hand over almost all our clothing, and they tried -- what they wanted to do was to search us, to frisk us in detail. I had to take all my clothes off, except my underwear, and they sent all of us up onto the stage. I was sent up there too, and they hit me with some sort of iron bar or pipe. Anyway, it was metal and round in shape. And from that blow, I might have gone a step or two forward unconsciously, and then I returned. I took several steps back because I was afraid that they would beat me again, that they would beat me more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From -- in the period between Bajram day and the holiday called Vidovdan Day, were more people being killed inside -- were more people that were detained in the room killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, not during that period from Bajram until Vidovdan or St. Vitez Day, but on one occasion a group came in, whether it was Zoks' group or a mixed group I'm not quite sure, and they also beat us and would draw -- or, rather, cut into our skin the four "S" signs on our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What would they cut the sign with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they cut that on the back of everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, just one person. They carved the four "S" signs on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were -- no, sorry, you've already answered that. I'm sorry. If we move now, then, to Vidovdan day, would you describe to us what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Bajram, after that period when the first group of people were killed, perhaps the following day or something like that, I don't remember the exact time, a person turned up, calling out my name, and I knew them. And the person was in police uniform, and I asked for assistance to protect my father, if not me. And he said that the key that was there somewhere in the SUP in Celopek or wherever and that an intervention was already made and the key would no longer be there, but it would be in the SUP of the Zvornik Municipality so that nobody would be able to enter without a permit or something like that. So nobody entered at that time. Nobody was able to enter through the door because the key wasn't there, since the door wasn't open. And that day, during that time when Repic turned up, the door happened to be open because that was the time when we were brought our food. It was lunchtime. It was about 2.00 or 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, somewhere around there. Anyway, he came in with an automatic rifle and once again asked us to talk or anyone to tell him about the people that he was looking for. He wanted us to tell him. Now, some people began talking, and he shot them straight away. After that, he shot a burst of gunfire above our heads, and I was on that side, and four people dropped down to the floor. They fell. Three were injured, three were wounded, and two were able to get up. The third one stayed lying down, and that was the person whose sex organ had been cut off. He came up to him and shot him with his pistol, and said that as far as he was concerned, he didn't want any wounded people. So then he went back to where he was standing in front of us and once again asked us who could tell him what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if you would rather that we stopped, because obviously you're extremely moved ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked us once again if we could tell him anything. However, the people were all in a panic by that time, and they started shouting and saying that if anybody knew anything, they should move over to the other side, that we should tell him what we knew. And we were all fully aware that he would shoot us. Then there was another burst of gunfire. He shot again, and he ordered us to cross over from one side of the room to the other, where he shot a burst of gunfire again. And I think that on the spot, he killed about 20 people. There were 22 people or maybe 24 people who were wounded, of which of those wounded two people died in that same room, succumbing to the wounds. After that, he said that we had to clean all the mess up and that he would return in about half an hour, and that it all had to be clean, and not leave any traces. And then he ordered us to sing the song he told us to sing at the beginning. Whether he wrote the song or whatever, I don't know, but we had to sing the song while we were cleaning everything up and taking everything out, to leave the room clean and clear of all the traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1067 [sic] -- excuse me, 1065, I'll ask if we can go to page 4 of the exhibit that's on the screen. I would suggest that maybe we take a ten-minute break at this stage, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Marcussen, you have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, if you would look at the screen, are the names of the killed and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please check why Mr. Seselj does not receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm receiving it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: VS-1065, are there -- are there names of the deceased and wounded people that you talked about, are they shown on the screen at the moment? And I'd like the Registrar just to move the picture up just a little bit so we get the last names. I think that's good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can go into private session for a very brief moment again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 1065, after this, were you -- were the people from Celopek moved to be detained in another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a day or two -- a day or two later after what had happened in Celopek, those of us who remained there, who remained alive and wounded, were transferred to the old prison in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how long, approximately, did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately a fortnight to 20 days, I don't quite remember, in those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And about how many people from -- that you had been detained with at Celopek were with you at the jail in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 80, maybe a few more. That was the number, roughly, in the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And after having been detained in the jail in Zvornik, were you taken somewhere else, where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some time, after we'd spent some time in Zvornik in the old jail, they told us that we should make a list of everybody wounded and injured. We didn't know why. And those who weren't wounded or injured, after we'd made up that list, compiled that list, we were taken out a few days later and transported by bus to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- in the interests of time, I will -- and for the sake of the witness, I will stop with the witness at this point. With respect to the exhibit that's on the screen, I propose that we remove the last page, as I'm not going to discuss the particular victims that are mentioned there. So we will, from the Prosecution -- sorry, we'll ask the Registrar if the Registrar would be kind enough to remove the last page of this exhibit, and then this will end the direct examination of the witness. Now, I have a proofing note that was drafted up and has now been translated that I would like to hand over to the accused in English and B/C/S. Obviously, as the accused has not had this before -- sorry, I was looking at the wrong thing. I, of course, understand if the accused needs until tomorrow to digest the proofing note and do the cross-examination of that tomorrow, but at least we managed to get the proofing note done. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, I would not want to evoke such painful memories again, but as a judge there are some items I would like to shed light on. You said that your father was among the casualties. Was his body found, or as of now do you still not know where your father's body is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was he buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is buried where we lived before, in our village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was his body found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly, but I think it was at Crni Vrh, in the mass grave there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You talked at length about Mr. Dusan Repic. Have you ever -- did you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think his name was Dusan Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few years ago, I heard talk that there were legal proceedings in Sabac against him, and I think he admitted to killing 15 people in Celopek. And afterwards, there was a trial in Belgrade for the six accused that I mentioned. He was one of them. And I think he's in prison now. That was the information I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, are you ready to start with the cross-examination, after having read the proofing note?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that this witness testified truthfully. I am sorry for the tragedy that he has had in his life, and I'm not going to ask him any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll ask my fellow Judges if they have any questions to put to the witness. Very well. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague, on the Prosecution's request, and we of course extend all our condolences for this tragedy you've lived through. So we really feel very sorry for what happened to you and extend our condolences. We wish you all the best for your return home. We'll now adjourn so that you may leave this courtroom. Because there is an audience in the gallery, we'll have to close the curtains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, tomorrow we have the videos, I guess, as our schedule is concerned, so we'll see the videos tomorrow. And obviously we will have no hearing on Thursday. Mr. Marcussen, I would like you and Mr. Mundis to check thoroughly the schedule for the witnesses to come. After May 5th, please check that everything is on track and that we won't run into any problems, as far as the scheduled witnesses are concerned. And if for any reason one witness was not available, please try to have a backup programme in store, which means, you know, that you need to have several witnesses ready to appear, inasmuch as Mr. Seselj could also cross-examine adequately and is well prepared for that. But we'll see -- we'll check this on a case-by-case basis. Mr. Seselj, we have some time left, and I would like to know whether there's some items that you would like to discuss.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I have a number of administrative matters to raise. First of all, I've just received these notes from the interview of VS-1065, and last week the Prosecution said, bearing in mind the situation that I'm in in the Detention Unit, that it would provide me with a set of the relevant documents relating to that particular witness. However, from these notes I see for the first time now that this witness, on the 16th of August, 1993, talked to members of the centre of the security services, I assume of the Muslim authorities; but I don't know where, was it in Tuzla or somewhere else? I didn't have that document in my possession. Of course, even if I did have it, my position would be identical and I would not cross-examine this witness, because apart from some matters of quantification and some details that you noticed, too, during the examination-in-chief, I don't have anything to challenge on the whole, in view of that testimony. I knew even before that killings did happen in that place and that sexual abuse took place as well. However, I have to criticise this manner on the part of the Prosecution whereby I was not given -- provided with the sets of documents. So that is my first objection and first comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, it would appear that the accused -- or, rather, that the person in question met security services in 1993. The accused would have liked to obtain those documents, and he is once again complaining of the fact that the Prosecutor did not disclose this information to him. Would you have anything to tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. According to our records, the document was -- actually, the first in the bundle of documents that were disclosed on the 17th of April with receipt number 325, which was the bundle of material that was disclosed together with the other statements and the transcripts of the witness' testimony in previous cases. So this material was disclosed on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Seselj, apparently the bundle was communicated or disclosed to you on the 17th of April, and the receipt even bears a number, number 325. I don't know if this is the case, but this is what Mr. Marcussen told us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not impossible, Mr. President, because I received an official note having to do with this witness, which is just a few sentences long. But that's not the statement. There's no witness signature here. So it's not a report on the interview, it's just an official note. And in our police force, the practice is when an official note is compiled, the witness doesn't have to sign, it's just a piece of information. But when the witness gives a statement, then he signs. So this is a misunderstanding, I assume, because I did receive this official note, and it doesn't contain anything specific, nothing special, except an identification of Dusan Vuckovic, Repic, but then it's not a statement. Then I withdraw the objection if Mr. Marcussen had this in mind, but we had to clear the matter up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to confirm, this is what I had in mind, and that's all that I'm aware of that the Prosecution have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second comment is this, Judges: The question of relevance in calling this witness at all. The witness did testify about horrendous things, but you heard at the beginning of the examination-in-chief that he was testifying about the events of the 26th of May or from the 26th of May onwards, and he is testifying -- or he testified about the bestial behaviour of members of the Yellow Wasps. And I think the OTP -- it's up to the OTP to prove that before the 26th of April, 1992, that is to say, one month prior to that, that after that date a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party remained in Zvornik. They would have to prove that, and to prove that the Yellow Wasps have anything to do with the Serbian Radical Party and me, personally, at all, because otherwise there's no sense to all this. And I think the question of relevance, you, as the Trial Chamber, should raise at this point. I know that this is a very vivid example of the crimes that took place. These crimes cannot be justified by anything, although identical crimes were committed on the other side. But, of course, one crime does not justify another crime. I agree with that. But let's see what that has got to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, that is why the Trial Chamber requested from the Prosecution to obtain a copy of the indictment of the Belgrade trial, so that we can make sure that we understand exactly what's going on. I have to tell you that at the present time between the Radical Serb Party, yourself, and the Yellow Wasps, I am in a total mist or a fog. We have to establish a link. In fact, maybe we will hear other witnesses. We might get this document. You, yourself, will call your own witnesses to shed some light on this whole matter. But for the time being, I must say that we are in the dark, and we are trying to establish some kind of link or guiding light. For the time being, we didn't get any further precision, and this is why the Trial Chamber did not insist. Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, we will of course provide further evidence on this particular issue. As Your Honour and the accused knows, we are filling up the schedule with witnesses that are becoming available, and what is happening at the moment is that we're having crime-base Zvornik witnesses being moved up to fill gaps in the schedule, so we haven't had a possibility of presenting our evidence with respect to this crime site in any coherent way. We are fully aware of the problems that arise from the fact that we have to basically throw in witnesses in the middle of the sequence of other evidence. We, of course, regret that. We would have liked to present our case in a more coherent fashion, but for practical reasons that has not been possible. As a legal point, I would stress that if the accused has objections to the relevance of a piece of evidence, those objections should be made before the evidence is presented. It has been clear all the way along what this witness' evidence would be with respect to the events he has just testified about, so objections to relevance should have been made early on. I think it would not be appropriate for me to make submissions on the issue of relevance before we've actually had the evidence presented to the Court, but obviously it is our position that the crimes committed in the different detention facilities in the Zvornik areas were part of the overall plan that this case is about. And we're also going to present evidence about the link between the specific individuals mentioned as perpetrators and the accused. That will come hopefully in a more coherent fashion later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, what is your next point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, late last week I was informed about the appearance of this witness, and I only had the weekend to look through the material relating to this witness. So I didn't have a chance to indicate that the testimony was not relevant. You noticed, when the Prosecutor was putting certain leading questions in an impermissible way, I didn't wish to intervene, bearing in mind the really difficult situation the witness is in. But I think it is quite clear to everyone that the main problem here is relevance and that the Prosecution, even though it is in such a critical situation regarding witnesses, it must produce certain links and produce the results of its investigations. They must prove that a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, after the 26th of April, was in Zvornik. And I have produced documents showing that we attacked the Yellow Wasps in public because of their criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to hear the translation until the end. What you just told us now, you've already told this before, so we understand your point of view. Would you like to raise another topic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing further to add regarding this issue. What I would like to underline is the question of the book by Carla Del Ponte, and I am waiting your official position. One can see that there's a serious violation of the Statute and the Rules of the International Tribunal. Clearly, she was exposed to pressure to act in a certain way. She was not independent, as the Prosecutor, and I think there are certain consequences that follow. On the other hand, I draw your attention to the fact that I haven't heard anyone officially reacting on behalf of the Tribunal regarding lies spread in Belgrade that I met here in prison with the counsel of Haradinaj, Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Seselj. I will answer, but in tackling the last subject. With regards to the meetings that you may have had with the Haradinaj lawyers, I've asked the legal officer to check with the prison authorities to see if you, indeed, had had some contacts, and the Detention Unit replied that you had no contacts, indeed. So you would not have been able to meet Haradinaj's attorneys, so that is to answer the latter part of your intervention. With regards now to the first part regarding the book that Mrs. Carla Del Ponte wrote, at the present I haven't read this book yet. Aside from some press clippings, I do not know what this book contains. You're saying, "I'm expecting the Trial Chamber to adopt a position." I don't know what position you want us to adopt. We would have be able to identify exactly what is your request. What do you want us to do, exactly? In order for the Trial Chamber to take a position, to take a stand, or to have a position, it would be important that your request be identified clearly. The Prosecutor has to also reply, and then the Trial Chamber has to render a decision. I do not know at this point in time what do you request of us, exactly. Could you please be a little more precise, if you wish. You can make an oral submission, if you wish, but you can also present a written submission, registered in due form, and the Trial Chamber will reply to this written motion. The Prosecutor will also submit his comments. So at this point in time, I do not understand exactly what you want from us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
